newsitem.title: FRANCE: Better delay euro if no stability pact -Schroeder.
newsitem.headline: Better delay euro if no stability pact -Schroeder.

text.p: German Social Democrat Gerhard Schroeder said in an interview to be published on Thursday in French daily Le Figaro that it would be better to delay the launch of the euro single currency if it was not tied to a budget stability pact.
"If the adoption of the euro in 1999 cannot be reconciled with the signing of a stability pact, it would be better to wait," Schroder was quoted as saying in the interview.
An advance copy of the interview was supplied to Reuters.

Schroeder, seen as a potential candidate for chancellor from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said governments could be tempted to intervene to boost their economies at a time when 18 million people were unemployed in the European Union, but that budget stability was primordial.

"With 18 million jobless in Europe, (EU) countries should intervene to boost the economy. But safeguarding stability to achieve European monetary union prohibits us from doing that," he was quoted as saying.
"Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer is not the only one attached to the stability of the currency...it would be an enormous error to sacrifice stability," he said.
Schroeder has called in the past for a delay to the euro's launch if needed.
"I do not believe we have to speak of the end of Europe if the euro does not come in 1999," he said, stressing that German people were strongly attached to a strong German currency.
Schroeder also took a hard line on the independence of the future European central bank and warned against any political interference.
"The worst thing that could happen to us would be to subject the European central bank in Frankfurt to politicial uncertainties," he said.
In the case where the stability pact was not signed and sealed, Schroeder said he favoured a "controlled delay" of the single currency's launch.
"Saying that we will ease the criteria with French backing would amount to ignoring the particularities of Germany," he said.

France's new left-wing government has asked for time to reflect on the EU budget stability pact on control of deficits after the euro's launch and asked for the debate on monetary union to be widened to promote growth and employment.
Its call for more time to reflect has cast doubt on whether the stability pact can be signed by EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
